cards.title: The capacity region of the general two-user interference channel
cards.formal: Determine the capacity region C(W) for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel W, with independent private messages, separate encoders and no feedback, using the average-error operational model below. The additional requirement intended by “determine” or “characterize” remains to be specified: a general limiting formula is already known.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved network-information-theory model in which independent communications compete through interference.

progress.text: Han–Kobayashi establish a general achievable region, without a matching converse for every interference channel.
A general information-spectrum formula is given using limiting input-process quantities; the intended benchmark must distinguish its target from this known characterization.
A primary study of entangled transmitters explicitly leaves the general unassisted classical capacity question open.
An equivalence result for state information does not compute the underlying general network capacity regions.

cards.definitions: Let X₁,X₂,Y₁,Y₂ be arbitrary nonempty finite sets and let W(y₁,y₂|x₁,x₂)≥0 sum to 1 over (y₁,y₂) for each input pair. At block length n≥1 the conditional output distribution is the product over t=1,…,n of W(y₁,t,y₂,t|x₁,t,x₂,t). A code has positive integer message counts M₁,M₂, deterministic encoders f_i:{1,…,M_i}→X_i^n, and decoders g_i:Y_i^n→{1,…,M_i}. Messages U₁,U₂ are independent and uniform on their respective sets. Encoder i knows U_i only, and receiver i observes only Y_i^n and must reconstruct U_i. Both codes and W are known in advance to all terminals. There is no feedback, message cooperation, shared entanglement, common message, input-cost constraint or extra communication. Private means individually intended; secrecy from the other receiver is not required. The average joint error is P[g₁(Y₁^n)≠U₁ or g₂(Y₂^n)≠U₂], averaged over both uniform messages and the channel law. Its convergence to zero is equivalent to convergence of each receiver’s average error to zero. A nonnegative pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with n→∞, joint error tending to zero and liminf (log₂ M_i)/n≥R_i for i=1,2. C(W) is the closure in R² of all achievable pairs. Rates are bits per channel use. Arbitrarily large codebooks and unlimited computation are permitted; this is a capacity question, not an efficient encoding question. Maximizing error over message pairs defines a different convention and is not imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: The operational object C(W) is defined, but a completed benchmark criterion must specify the required representation or evaluability of its general characterization. Any proposed capacity theorem must prove both that all rates in its stated region are achievable and that rates outside it are impossible for every channel in the stated family. Merely repeating the operational definition or the known unrestricted information-spectrum formula does not identify the missing intended advance; the source must determine the additional requirement.

context_blocks.title: Two links share one medium
context_blocks.text: There are two senders and two receivers. Each sender has its own message, but both inputs can affect both outputs. If Y₁=X₁ and Y₂=X₂ for binary inputs, each link can independently send one bit per use, giving a square rate region. If instead both receivers see only X₁ XOR X₂, the two separate one-bit messages cannot both be recovered at a total rate above one bit per use. The tradeoff between the two rates, rather than either isolated link’s capacity, is the object of interest.

context_blocks.title: What reliable communication means
context_blocks.text: A code uses the channel many times and permits a small probability of decoding error. A rate is achievable when that error can tend to zero while the transmitted message counts grow exponentially with block length at the requested rates. The receivers need not reconstruct the other sender’s message. Conversely, “private message” does not prohibit that receiver from learning it: secrecy is an additional condition absent here.

context_blocks.title: Inner and outer bounds
context_blocks.text: An achievable region proves that particular pairs of rates can be supported. An outer bound proves that no code can operate outside a specified region. Han and Kobayashi’s 1981 result is a central inner bound; it is not a matching capacity theorem for every discrete memoryless interference channel. Exact results for special interference conditions do not cover arbitrary channel laws. The January 2025 primary discussion explicitly retains the general classical problem.

context_blocks.title: A general formula already exists
context_blocks.text: Ma and coauthors give an information-spectrum characterization using sequences of input distributions across unbounded block lengths. Their Theorem 1 describes a union of rate rectangles determined by limiting information quantities. This is mathematically more than the informal statement that capacity consists of achievable rates, but it still involves an unrestricted optimization over input processes. The authors explicitly distinguish this general formula from an easily computed characterization. Consequently, the inherited instruction to “characterize the region” needs a more precise acceptance requirement before it becomes a complete benchmark.

context_blocks.title: Related results use different assumptions
context_blocks.text: The Gaussian interference-channel card studies real-valued signals, Gaussian noise and power constraints; it is a separate channel family. The entanglement-assisted 2025 paper adds a resource absent from the present model. Lapidoth, Ni and Wang’s April 2026 theorem compares causal and noncausal state information in bipartite networks and explicitly does so without computing their capacity regions. None supplies the missing general, evaluable classical characterization.

notes: Specified the finite classical channel law, independent messages, separate codes, average error and asymptotic rates.
Compared the source’s wording with the existing 2013 general information-spectrum theorem.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The source asks to “characterize” the capacity region but does not specify what form of answer would improve on the existing operational definition or general information-spectrum formula. A finite-dimensional single-letter expression, a computable approximation procedure with a certified error bound, and an unrestricted limiting formula are different requirements. The source does not select one or prescribe encodings for numerical evaluation; choosing one here would create an additional mathematical target.
statement_review.scope: Individual model and source review; acceptance requirement unresolved; no independent proof audit.

sentences: The channel has two independent senders whose signals can interfere at two separate receivers.
Its capacity region consists of the two communication rates attainable with vanishing average decoding error over long blocks.
Known general inner bounds do not supply a matching converse for every finite channel law.
An unrestricted information-spectrum formula already exists and need not be easy to evaluate.
The source must therefore specify what additional form or evaluability its requested characterization requires.

changes: Defined the classical average-error capacity region and explained rate tradeoffs with binary channels.
Distinguished an inner bound, a general limiting formula and an evaluable characterization.
Retained the missing answer-format requirement instead of certifying an invented replacement.
Checked the 2025 unassisted context and the distinct April 2026 state-information theorem.
quality_review.scope: Checked the statement, model, answer criterion, context, significance and cited results; searched for subsequent work. Searches are not exhaustive, and paper proofs were not independently verified.

cards.context:
There are two senders and two receivers. Each sender has its own message, but both inputs can affect both outputs. If Y₁=X₁ and Y₂=X₂ for binary inputs, each link can independently send one bit per use, giving a square rate region. If instead both receivers see only X₁ XOR X₂, the two separate one-bit messages cannot both be recovered at a total rate above one bit per use. The tradeoff between the two rates, rather than either isolated link’s capacity, is the object of interest.

A code uses the channel many times and permits a small probability of decoding error. A rate is achievable when that error can tend to zero while the transmitted message counts grow exponentially with block length at the requested rates. The receivers need not reconstruct the other sender’s message. Conversely, “private message” does not prohibit that receiver from learning it: secrecy is an additional condition absent here.

An achievable region proves that particular pairs of rates can be supported. An outer bound proves that no code can operate outside a specified region. Han and Kobayashi’s 1981 result is a central inner bound; it is not a matching capacity theorem for every discrete memoryless interference channel. Exact results for special interference conditions do not cover arbitrary channel laws. The January 2025 primary discussion explicitly retains the general classical problem.

Ma and coauthors give an information-spectrum characterization using sequences of input distributions across unbounded block lengths. Their Theorem 1 describes a union of rate rectangles determined by limiting information quantities. This is mathematically more than the informal statement that capacity consists of achievable rates, but it still involves an unrestricted optimization over input processes. The authors explicitly distinguish this general formula from an easily computed characterization. Consequently, the inherited instruction to “characterize the region” needs a more precise acceptance requirement before it becomes a complete benchmark.

The Gaussian interference-channel card studies real-valued signals, Gaussian noise and power constraints; it is a separate channel family. The entanglement-assisted 2025 paper adds a resource absent from the present model. Lapidoth, Ni and Wang’s April 2026 theorem compares causal and noncausal state information in bipartite networks and explicitly does so without computing their capacity regions. None supplies the missing general, evaluable classical characterization.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
